description: Onatah is the corn spirit of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), one of the Three Sisters who sustain the people with the bean and squash spirits. A jealous rival, sometimes named Tawiscara, kidnapped her and hid her underground, bringing famine until her sisters freed her. The three crops are still planted together, a living lesson in cooperation.
source: native-languages.org — Onatah Corn Spirit; Haudenosaunee oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Corn Spirit of the Haudenosaunee, one of the Three Sisters (corn, beans, squash). Records of the story appear among the Seneca, Cayuga, Mohawk, Oneida, and Onondaga; the Three Sisters belong to the Deohako, the 'life supporters.' Some versions name the kidnapper Tawiscara or Hahgwehdaetgah, and the rescue by the other sisters restores the harvest. Cognate corn beings include Selu, Mondamin, and the Corn Mother. The record's Iroquois attribution is correct.

description: Oniare is the great horned water serpent of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), said to lurk in lakes and rivers, capsizing canoes and sending storms against the unwary. The Mohawk word onyare means 'snake,' and Onyarekowa, the great snake, was feared for its poisonous breath. It is the eternal enemy of the Thunderers, and offerings were once made to appease it.
source: native-languages.org — Oniare Horned Serpent; Haudenosaunee oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the great horned water serpent of the Iroquois. In Mohawk, onyare means 'snake' and Onyarekowa 'great snake'; the being has many recorded names including Angont, Djodi'kwado, and Jotéhkwatöh. It dwells in the Great Lakes, capsizes canoes, and is the mortal enemy of the thunder god Hinon (Heno). Offerings were made to gain its favor. Related great serpents include the Cherokee Uktena and Algonquian Maneto. The Iroquois attribution is correct.

description: Okwa Naholo, 'white people of the water,' are supernatural beings of Choctaw tradition who dwell in deep pools and springs. Recorded by Henry S. Halbert in the nineteenth century, they are described with light skins like the underside of a trout, and they seize swimmers, who after three days can no longer leave the water. Some traditions set their home beneath the Abita River.
source: Access Genealogy — Okwa Naholo (after Halbert); Choctaw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested in the 19th-century fieldwork of Henry S. Halbert on Choctaw beliefs, describing the Okwa Nahola ('white people of the water') who dwell in deep pools, have skins light like a trout's, and capture humans, converting them into beings like themselves. The tribe is correctly given as Choctaw. Variant spelling Oka Nahullo appears in the same records.

description: The olobit, also called the 'sharp-breasted snake,' is a monstrous serpent of the Natchez, a people of the lower Mississippi. Described in John R. Swanton's field research, it is a supernatural reptile closely related to the Uktena of the Cherokee and other great serpents of the Southeast.
source: Swanton, 'Myths and Tales of the Southeastern Indians'; native-languages.org
research_notes: Attested in Natchez folklore as olo'bit, the walking terrapin, and intsiyacdoo'cgu, the 'sharp-breasted snake,' with the Cherokee ukteni named as a close counterpart. Swanton collected the material among the Natchez, and the serpent shares the lethal, supernatural character of other Southeastern great serpents. The Natchez attribution is correct.

description: Not independently attested in any recorded Native American tradition. No ethnographer, tribal history, or published collection describes a being named Nakshimo, and the name appears in none of the standard references for North American folklore. The entry appears to be a garbled or invented figure.
source: No source found; absent from ethnographic literature
research_notes: Searches of native-languages.org, ethnographic references, and general folklore indexes produced no attestation for a spirit named Nakshimo. The record carries no tribe and only a generic USA label, which is typical of fabricated entries in this series. No safe analogue could be matched to the name.

description: Nanabush, also called Nanabozho, Wenabozho, or Waynaboozhoo, is the great culture hero and trickster of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe, Odawa, Potawatomi) and many Algonquian nations. A shapeshifter born of a mortal mother and the West Wind, he remade the world after a great flood and taught the people how to live. His tales are told in winter and carry both laughter and sacred teaching.
source: native-languages.org — Nanabozho; Anishinaabe aadizookaan tradition
research_notes: Nanabush (Nanabozho/Wenabozho) is a fully attested culture hero of the Anishinaabe and neighboring Algonquian nations across Canada and the northern United States. A trickster-transformer often pictured as a hare, he recreated the world on a turtle's back after the flood, using a muskrat's pawful of earth. Winter is the traditional season for telling his aadizookaanan (sacred stories). The Canada attribution is correct.

description: Nanabush, known in his many nations as Nanabozho or Wenabozho, is the culture hero and trickster of the Anishinaabe and neighboring Algonquian peoples whose lands span the Great Lakes on both sides of the United States-Canada border. Through his adventures he remade the world and taught the people to live. His stories, told when snow covers the ground, mix comedy and sacred instruction.
source: native-languages.org — Nanabozho; Anishinaabe aadizookaan tradition
research_notes: This USA record duplicates the Canadian Nanabush entry and is likewise fully attested; Anishinaabe homelands in Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Ontario make the being legitimately part of both countries' traditions. Same figure as the Ojibwe Wenabozho who battled Mishibizhiw the Great Lynx. Keep both entries, attributing to the Anishinaabe rather than any single country.

description: Nanook is the master of polar bears in Inuit tradition, the great bear who decides whether a hunter succeeds. When a bear is killed, its hide is hung in a place of honor within the igloo and stays there for several days, and small offerings, tools for the bear's soul, are made so that its spirit will return. Such respect keeps the hunting balance between humans and the animals that sustain them.
source: Wikipedia — Nanook; Inuit oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Inuit master of bears who determines hunting success. The hide is given a place of honor in the igloo for a set period, and offerings of tools for the bear's soul (tatkoit) are made so the animal returns to be hunted again. The Canada attribution is correct. Some popular accounts conflate Nanook with unrelated sky or moon figures, which this entry avoids.

description: Not independently attested in any recorded Native American tradition of the United States. No published ethnography, tribal narrative, or reference work documents a spirit called the Nash Bear, and the entry appears to be an invented or garbled figure. Honoring the bear as a powerful relative, however, is genuinely widespread across Algonquian, Siouan, and Iroquoian nations alike.
source: No source found; absent from ethnographic literature
research_notes: No attestation found for a 'Nash Bear' in any US tribal tradition or published reference. The record carries no tribe, only a generic USA label. While bear-spirit beliefs are genuinely common (clan ancestors, healers, guardians), no named Nash Bear exists; the entry appears fabricated.

description: Not independently attested in any recorded Canadian First Nations tradition. No published collection or tribal account documents a spirit named the Nash Bear, and the entry appears to be invented or garbled. Across Canada, however, the bear is a deeply honored being: a clan ancestor, medicine spirit, and guardian among nations such as the Cree, Ojibwe, and Coast Salish.
source: No source found; absent from ethnographic literature
research_notes: No attestation found for a 'Nash Bear' in any Canadian First Nations source; the record carries no tribe, only a generic Canada label. Genuine bear-spirit traditions exist across Canada but none by this name, so the entry appears fabricated. This record duplicates nashbear-usa.

description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne tradition; no recorded Cheyenne narrative describes a 'Night Stalker.' The closest attested beings of the night are the Nightspirits, 'Those Who Walk in Darkness,' of the Ho-Chunk, who spread darkness as they walk and grant war blessings to vision seekers. The entry appears to conflate these figures or to invent a Cheyenne counterpart.
source: No Cheyenne source found; cf. Hotcak Encyclopedia (Ho-Chunk Nightspirits)
research_notes: No recorded Cheyenne figure matches a 'Night Stalker'; the name appears in no Cheyenne source. The Ho-Chunk Nightspirits (Hok'áwas Mąnį́na, 'Those Who Walk in Darkness') are genuinely attested as darkness-bringing spirits who bless vision seekers, but they are Ho-Chunk, not Cheyenne. The entry appears to be a fabricated or misattributed figure.

description: Nikommo belongs to the little people of Wampanoag tradition rather than to the giants. The attested Wampanoag giants are Maushop and his sons, whose struggles with the dangerous little people of the dawnland are told along the Massachusetts coast. Nikommo is better understood as one of those small, capricious forest beings, akin to the pukwudgies of neighboring Algonquian nations.
source: native-languages.org — Wampanoag legends; Massachusetts oral tradition
research_notes: The record's 'giant' type is a mislabel: in Wampanoag tradition the giant is Maushop (Moshup), while Nikommo is one of the little people, capricious forest beings akin to the pukwudgies. The two classes were confused in this entry. Attestation is thin but the little-people class is genuine among the Wampanoag.

description: Nokomis, 'my grandmother' in Anishinaabemowin, is the wise grandmother of Nanabush in Ojibwe tradition, the elder who raises the culture hero and counsels him through his adventures. Her name and role appear across the Anishinaabe nations of the Great Lakes, and she is a figure of kindness, humor, and steady guidance. Longfellow popularized her as Hiawatha's grandmother.
source: native-languages.org — Nokomis; Wikipedia — Nokomis
research_notes: Attested as the grandmother of Wenabozho (Nanabush) among the Anishinaabe; nookomis is literally 'my grandmother' in Anishinaabemowin. Cognate grandmother figures include Nukumi of the Mi'kmaq and Grandmother Woodchuck of the Abenaki. This USA record duplicates record 20 (nokomis, Ojibwe); both describe the same attested being.

description: The northern lights, called wâwâhtêwak, 'those that go in circles,' in Cree, are seen as spirits dancing across the winter sky. Some nations say they are the ghosts of the departed holding a great dance, and the Cree phrase cîpayak kâ-nîmihitocik, 'the ghosts are dancing,' names the display directly. Whistling at the lights is forbidden, for it offends the dancers and draws them down.
source: Cree Literacy Network — 'The Northern Lights'; Cree oral tradition
research_notes: Attested in Cree tradition: wâwâhtêwak, 'those that go in circles,' are spirit dancers in the sky, and cîpayak kâ-nîmihitocik means 'the ghosts are dancing.' Whistling at them is taboo, as it may offend or summon them. The Canada attribution is correct; the same spirit-dance reading recurs across northern nations (Dene, Innu, Inuit).

description: The name nu-u has no independent attestation, but it corresponds most closely to the water babies of Great Basin tradition, known to the Southern Paiute as pit-u-u or paúngaa'a. These small, crying beings guard springs and lakes and aid shamans, but are dangerous to those who approach their waters. Their weeping is a warning, and children are taught to keep away from deep water where they live.
source: Wikipedia — Water Babies (Paiute pit-u-u); Great Basin oral tradition
research_notes: The exact name nu-u is unattested, but it closely matches pit-u-u, the Southern Paiute water baby, a small crying being that guards springs and serves shamans. Similar beings exist among the Ute (pawapicts), Washoe, Western Shoshone (nu-numbi), and Yokuts (paakniwat). The entry is best understood as a garbled reference to these attested water babies.

description: Nûñnë'hï is James Mooney's spelling of Nunnehi, the Cherokee word for a race of immortal spirit people, 'those who live anywhere,' who dwell in the mountains and forests of the old Cherokee country. Usually invisible and kindly, they sometimes appeared to warn their people, and during the Removal they were said to have sheltered Cherokee families in a cave whose door closed against the soldiers.
source: Wikipedia — Nunnehi; Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee'
research_notes: Nûñnë'hï is Mooney's orthographic rendering of the attested Cherokee Nunnehi, the immortal spirit people distinct from ghosts and gods. They warned the people and, per tradition, hid families from the Removal in a cave closed by a stone door. This record duplicates record 21 (nunnehi-cherokee); both describe the same being and should be kept as variants.

description: Naiyenezgani, 'Monster Slayer' or 'Killer of Enemies,' is the elder of the Hero Twins of the Navajo, with a Chiricahua Apache cognate, Naaghéé'neesgháné, often rendered 'Killer of Enemies.' The Navajo hero is a warrior of unmatched strength, while the Apache counterpart is often comic and cowardly. Both twins rid the world of the monsters that plagued the first people.
source: Wikipedia — Nayenezgani; Apache and Navajo oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Navajo Naayéé' Neizghání ('Monster Slayer'), elder of the Hero Twins. The record's Apache tag is defensible via the Chiricahua Apache cognate Naaghéé'neesgháné ('Killer of Enemies'), who is often comically cowardly rather than heroic. This is the same family of beings as Naiye' of the White Mountain Apache (see record 18).

description: Naiye' is the devouring giant of White Mountain Apache tradition recorded by Pliny Earle Goddard in 1910. In the tale, the giant swallows the people's world; the twins born to the Sun's maiden then kill the monster, and from the Sun they receive the name Naiyenezgani, 'Monster Slayer.' The story is part of the origin cycle of the White Mountain Apache.
source: Goddard, 'Myths and Tales of the White Mountain Apache' (1910)
research_notes: Attested in Goddard's 1910 field collection (Gutenberg #53113): Naiye' is a devouring giant killed by the hero twins, one of whom then receives the name Naiyenezgani from the Sun. This gives an Apache-language provenance for the 'Monster Slayer' name. The White Mountain Apache attribution is correct and is supported by the primary text.

description: Naato'si is the sun deity of the Blackfoot, a name meaning 'holy one' rather than simply 'sun.' Created by the high god Apistotoke, he rules the sky with his wife, the moon Komorkis, and their children are the stars; his son Morning-Star is grandfather to the hero Star Boy (Poia). He is central to the Sun Dance, whose rites and sweat lodge came to the people through his gifts.
source: native-languages.org — Naato'si Sun God; Blackfoot oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Blackfoot sun deity; the name means 'holy one,' not literally 'sun,' a nuance often lost in translation. Created by Apistotoke, he is married to Komorkis (moon), father of Morning-Star, and grandfather of the Star Boy hero Poia. He is central to the Sun Dance, whose rituals were given through him. The Blackfoot attribution is correct.

description: Nokomis is the grandmother of Nanabush (Nanabozho) in Ojibwe tradition, her very name meaning 'my grandmother' in Anishinaabemowin. She raises the trickster culture hero after the death of his mother and guides him through his adventures. Cognate grandmother figures include Nukumi of the Mi'kmaq and Grandmother Woodchuck of the Abenaki. Longfellow popularized her as Hiawatha's grandmother.
source: native-languages.org — Nokomis; Wikipedia — Nokomis
research_notes: Attested as the Anishinaabe grandmother of Wenabozho (Nanabush); nookomis is literally 'my grandmother.' Cognates include Nukumi (Mi'kmaq) and Grandmother Woodchuck (Abenaki). The Ojibwe attribution is correct. This record duplicates nokomis-usa (record 13); both describe the same attested being.

description: The Nunnehi, meaning 'the travelers' or 'those who live anywhere,' are a race of immortal spirit people of the Cherokee, distinct from ghosts and from gods. They dwell in the mountains, forests, and stone houses of Cherokee country, are usually friendly, and sometimes showed themselves to warn of danger. During the Removal they were said to hide Cherokee families in a cave closed by a stone door.
source: Wikipedia — Nunnehi; Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee'
research_notes: Attested as the immortal spirit people of the Cherokee, whose name means 'those who live anywhere' or 'the people who live forever.' They are distinct from ghosts and gods, live in the mountains and stone houses, and warned the people of danger. During the Removal they sheltered families in a cave closed by a stone door. The Cherokee attribution is correct.

description: Nalusa Falaya, 'the long black being,' is a feared shadow creature of Choctaw tradition. Usually a tall, gaunt humanoid with small eyes and long pointed ears, it is said to slither like a snake or melt into dusk shadows, frightening children who stay out too late and waylaying lost hunters, sometimes passing on its harmful power with a thorn. Its young drift as small lights along the marsh.
source: native-languages.org; Wikipedia — Choctaw mythology (after Halbert); Bushnell 1910
research_notes: Attested in Choctaw tradition; the name means 'long black being.' Descriptions follow the 19th-century fieldwork of Henry S. Halbert and a 1910 account by David Bushnell Jr. recorded from Pisatuntema of the Louisiana Choctaw. It lurks in dusk shadows, frightens children and hunters, and may transfer harmful power. The Choctaw attribution is correct.

description: Nalusa Chito, also called Impa Shilup, 'the soul eater,' is the great black shadow being of Choctaw belief. It was said to creep inside a person who let evil thoughts or despair take hold, devouring the soul from within. Many in the Choctaw Nation avoid speaking its name for fear of drawing it, a practice recorded in the tribe's own traditions and in studies of Choctaw mythology.
source: Wikipedia — Choctaw mythology; HandWiki — Choctaw mythology
research_notes: Attested in Choctaw belief as Nalusa Chito, also Impa Shilup, the soul-eater, a great black being that creeps inside those who let evil thoughts or depression take hold and eats their souls. Many Choctaw people avoid saying the name lest the spirit be summoned. The record's Choctaw attribution and spirit type are correct.

description: The loup-garou of Acadian and French Canadian tradition is a werewolf, usually imagined as a shaggy dog or bear-like creature rather than a wolf. According to the Canadian Encyclopedia, it was understood as a curse, often the price of failing to perform Easter confession for years, and breakable by drawing its blood. Its tales are a Catholic moral lesson.
source: The Canadian Encyclopedia — Loup-garou
research_notes: Attested as the Acadian/French Canadian werewolf; the Canadian Encyclopedia describes a usually dog-like beast resulting from a curse, commonly the failure of Easter confession, breakable by drawing blood. It is milder than US and European versions. The record's 'warlock' label is a misnomer, but the loup-garou attribution is correct.

description: Water babies are small, crying beings of Great Basin and Plateau tradition, known among the Southern Paiute as pit-u-u and to other nations by related names. They guard springs, rivers, and lakes; some traditions say they are ghosts of infants who died in a famine, while others know them as spirit guardians who help shamans. Their weeping warns the unwary away from dangerous water.
source: Wikipedia — Water Babies; history.co.uk — Native American folklore
research_notes: Attested as a broad class of water beings across the Great Basin and Plateau, most fully documented among the Southern Paiute (pit-u-u) with cognates in Ute, Washoe, Shoshone, and Yokuts traditions. Some accounts make them ghosts of famine victims; others, spirit guardians who aid shamans. The USA attribution is correct.

description: Water spirits form one of the oldest and widest classes of Native American belief in the United States, though no single being bears the plain name 'water spirit.' Each nation has its own: the horned Underwater Panther of the Great Lakes and East, the water babies of the Great Basin, and the Okwa Naholo of the Choctaw. They guard waters, reward respect, and drown those who defy them.
source: Wikipedia — Underwater panther; Water Babies; Choctaw mythology
research_notes: A generic category rather than a single attested being; water spirits are documented across many US nations under specific names (Mishipeshu/Underwater Panther, water babies, Okwa Naholo, and others). The record's alias lists 'waterspirits-canada,' confirming the two entries are a split of one generic concept. Descriptions should name real constituent beings rather than a composite 'water spirit.'

description: Water spirits are a broad, attested class across Canada's First Nations, though each people knows them by its own names. Among them are the horned great lynx of the Anishinaabe, the water babies of the north, and the Naitaka of Okanagan Lake. They rule the rivers, lakes, and ocean, and ceremonies are offered to them for safe passage and for the harvests of the water.
source: Wikipedia — Underwater panther; Ogopogo; zhaawanart.com — Mishibizhiw
research_notes: A generic category; the specific attested beings include the Anishinaabe Mishibizhiw (great lynx/underwater panther), the water babies of northern tradition, and Naitaka, the Okanagan lake spirit. This entry is a Canadian split of the same generic concept as waterspirits-usa. Naming real beings keeps the description accurate.

description: Not independently attested in any recorded Canadian First Nations tradition. No tribal account or published source describes a spirit named Wee-kin, and the name appears to be invented or garbled. It may be a corruption of weyekin, the personal guardian spirit of the Nez Perce, or a generic Canadian entry; either way, no such being is documented in the folklore of Canada.
source: No source found; cf. Wikipedia — Weyekin (Nez Perce guardian spirit)
research_notes: No attestation found for 'Wee-kin' in any Canadian tradition. The phonetically closest real being is the Nez Perce weyekin, a personal guardian spirit gained on a vision quest, but the Nez Perce are a US Plateau nation and weyekin is not a named monster or Canadian spirit. The entry appears to be a garbled or fabricated name.

description: Not independently attested under the name Wee-Tent. The Ojibwe and other Anishinaabe peoples do tell of little people, known as Bagwajiwininiwag, 'the wilderness little Anishinaabe,' along with the water-dwelling memengwesi and the mischievous bajiine, but no source names one of them Wee-Tent. The entry appears to be a garbled or invented label for a genuine class of little forest spirits.
source: native-languages.org — Pukwudgie/Bagwajinini; zhaawanart.com
research_notes: The name Wee-Tent (or Wee-Tin) is unattested. The record's own summary describes an Ojibwe little person, a real class: the Bagwajiwininiwag ('wilderness little Anishinaabe'), with related beings memengwesi and bajiine. No source uses 'Wee-Tent.' The entry appears to be an invented label applied to a genuine Ojibwe little-people tradition.

description: The wendigo, also spelled windigo, is the cannibal spirit of the Algonquian-speaking peoples, from the Cree and Ojibwe of Canada to the Wampanoag and Pequot of New England. A human possessed by greed and hunger is said to become a gaunt, ice-hearted monster that devours human flesh and never fills its stomach. Scholars read it as a warning against greed and starvation.
source: The Canadian Encyclopedia; Wikipedia — Wendigo
research_notes: Attested across Algonquian nations including the Cree, Ojibwe/Chippewa, Potawatomi, Pequot, Narragansett, and Wampanoag. A cannibal spirit born of greed, gluttony, or taboo-breaking, sometimes imagined as a possessed human; its icy heart and endless hunger stand against the community's needs. The Canada attribution is correct, though the being spans the border.

description: Not independently attested in Shoshone tradition; the Shoshone, a Great Basin people, have no recorded whale ancestor-spirit, and the description of a guardian of the springs matches no documented being. The real water guardians of the Shoshone are the water babies, known as nu-numbi, who watch over springs and lakes. The entry combines an ocean creature with a desert water spirit.
source: Wikipedia — Water Babies (Western Shoshone nu-numbi)
research_notes: No Shoshone whale ancestor-spirit is recorded; the tribe has no ocean in its mythology. The attested Shoshone water guardians are the water babies (nu-numbi), who watch over springs. The entry is one of a series of five impossible whale attributions to inland or mountain peoples (records 31-35) and is a fabrication.

description: Not attested as a whale deity of the Cherokee. The Cherokee tell of the Dakwa, a great fish of the deep waters, whose name was later used in translations of the Bible for 'whale'; Mooney recorded 'The Hunter and the Dakwa,' a tale of a man swallowed and carried by the great fish, told by the storytellers Swimmer and Tagwaddihi. No whale god or cave guardian appears in Cherokee tradition.
source: Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee'; Smoky Mountain News — the Cherokee Dakwa
research_notes: No Cherokee whale deity is attested. The closest real figure is the Dakwa, a great fish used as the Cherokee word for 'whale' in Bible translation, appearing in Mooney's tale 'The Hunter and the Dakwa.' The entry's 'deity' and 'cave guardian' claims are unsupported; the whale series (31-35) is fabricated.

description: Not independently attested in Apache tradition. The Apache are a Southwestern people whose homelands hold no whales, and no recorded Apache narrative features a whale ghost or desert guardian. The documented supernatural beings of the Apache include the Water Monster and the holy people of their origin stories rather than any sea creature. The entry appears to be an invented figure.
source: No Apache source found; cf. Goddard, 'Myths and Tales of the White Mountain Apache'
research_notes: No whale appears in Apache tradition; the record is one of the fabricated whale series (31-35). Apache supernatural beings are documented (e.g., Water Monster, holy people of origin stories), none of which is a whale ghost. The 'guardian of the deserts' phrasing is a template fill that matches no attested being.

description: Not independently attested in Miwok tradition; the Miwok of California have no recorded whale ghost. The famous whale of California Indian literature is the Wintu tale of the Inland Whale, retold by Theodora Kroeber, a story of a young man swallowed by the great whale, not a ghost and not Miwok. The entry appears to combine a real coastal tale with a wrong tribe and a wrong creature.
source: Theodora Kroeber, 'The Inland Whale'; no Miwok source
research_notes: No Miwok whale ghost is attested. The real analogue is the Wintu folktale 'The Inland Whale,' collected and retold by Theodora Kroeber, in which a young man is swallowed by a whale and returns; it is a tale, not a ghost, and belongs to the Wintu, not the Miwok. Part of the fabricated whale series.

description: Not independently attested in Cheyenne tradition; the Cheyenne, a Plains people, have no recorded whale giant, and no source documents a whale in their mythology. The principal figures of Cheyenne tradition are the creator Maheo and the spider trickster Wihio. The entry appears to be an invented figure, one of a series of impossible whale attributions across desert and Plains nations.
source: No Cheyenne source found; cf. Cheyenne cosmology (Maheo, Wihio)
research_notes: No Cheyenne whale is attested; the tribe is a Plains nation without whale traditions. Real Cheyenne figures include Maheo the creator and Wihio the spider trickster. This closes the fabricated whale series (31-35), all of which attribute whales to tribes whose homelands and mythologies contain no such being.
